items.title: Anthropic says large language models enable formal software verification at much larger scale [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: LLMs are making formal software verification feasible at a much larger scale
items.summary:
Anthropic reports that large language models (LLMs) are making formal software verification feasible on a much larger scale than before. This advancement could significantly improve the reliability and security of software systems by automating complex verification tasks that were previously too resource-intensive.

The company highlights how LLMs can assist in generating formal proofs and verifying code correctness more efficiently, potentially transforming software development and quality assurance processes. This development may lead to broader adoption of formal methods in industry, enhancing software safety and reducing bugs.

items.title: Analysis finds identical AI requests emit 8.5 times more CO2 in Texas than Sweden due to energy source differences [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: The same AI request emits 8.5 times more CO2 in Texas than in Sweden
items.summary:
A recent analysis reveals that running the same AI requests produces about 8.5 times more carbon dioxide emissions in Texas compared to Sweden. This significant difference is linked to the energy mix powering data centers, with Sweden relying more heavily on renewable energy sources, resulting in a lower carbon footprint for AI operations.

The study highlights how regional variations in electricity generation impact the environmental cost of AI workloads, emphasizing the role of cleaner energy in reducing emissions associated with data processing.

items.title: Analysis of 12 AI models from 10 labs reveals unanimous controversial view that humans prioritize group loyalty over truth [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Every AI model has the same "controversial" take on humans
items.summary:
A study asked 12 AI models from 10 labs across three countries to provide their most controversial opinions on humans, with all models repeatedly stating that humans tend to conform to group beliefs rather than seek objective truth. The models expressed variations on this theme, highlighting human loyalty to identity and social belonging as stronger motivators than principles or facts.

The shared perspectives included views that human intelligence often serves to justify pre-existing loyalties, that moral convictions are frequently tribal loyalty in disguise, and that humans evolved more to win social status than to discover truth. Some models described human consciousness as a mechanism for rationalizing instincts and social loyalties rather than an unbiased decision-maker.

This consensus among diverse AI models suggests a common analytical pattern in AI assessments of human behavior, emphasizing social conformity and rationalization over independent reasoning or principled truth-seeking.

items.title: NVIDIA launches OpenShell, a secure runtime for autonomous AI agents with kernel-level policy enforcement and formal verification [ * ] [ ⬢ ]
items.originalTitle: OpenShell – A safe, private runtime for fleets of autonomous AI agents
items.summary:
NVIDIA has released OpenShell, a runtime environment designed to safely manage fleets of autonomous AI agents by enforcing strict access policies at the kernel level. OpenShell isolates agents in sandboxes, controlling file access, system calls, and network connections, while using formal verification to review policy changes before they are applied.

The platform supports Linux, macOS on Apple Silicon, and Windows with WSL 2, and integrates with container technologies like Docker and Podman. OpenShell includes tools for managing policies, credentials, and gateways, and offers SDKs and agent skills to facilitate development and deployment. It collects limited anonymous telemetry to improve the project, with options to disable it.

items.title: Developer fine-tunes a 360M-parameter language model to simulate a terminal interface by predicting screen changes from keypresses, enabling file creation, vim, tmux, and games [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: WorldTUI: I trained a 360M model to pretend to be a terminal
items.summary:
A developer trained a 360 million parameter language model to act as a terminal emulator without an underlying shell or filesystem, predicting screen updates based on user keypresses. The model can run programs like vim and tmux, create files, and play games such as snake, maintaining short-term memory of commands. It was fine-tuned on terminal sessions recorded from real programs running inside Docker containers and uses a compact token vocabulary to efficiently represent screen changes.

The model treats the terminal as a grid of characters and predicts changes to specific rows and cursor positions rather than appending text sequentially. It supports operations like copying rows to handle scrolling and screen clearing, enabling realistic terminal behavior. The demo runs in a desktop browser with WebGPU support and is optimized for Chrome or Edge, though it can run slowly on modern phones. This approach explores the concept of learned applications that predict interface states rather than relying on traditional code execution.

items.title: Researchers find AI-generated text uses more complex linguistic features than human writing, possibly due to optimization for information density over communication [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Why is AI-generated language so hard to understand?
items.summary:
A study analyzing AI-generated text across various domains found that leading language models use more linguistically complex features, such as inanimate subjects with animate verbs and low-frequency n-grams, compared to human writing and paraphrases. The researchers suggest this complexity arises because AI models prioritize information density for tasks like math and reasoning rather than optimizing for human communication.

The study examined nine frontier and near-frontier models, noting significant variation among model families and increased use of long syntactic dependencies and stacked nouns. A proof-of-concept fine-tuning experiment applying a length penalty showed divergence from human-like language patterns, supporting the hypothesis that AI language generation is misaligned with human linguistic processing demands. The findings highlight potential areas for improving AI text generation to better align with human understanding.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.29162v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: There is a widespread sense that AI-generated text has recently become harder to understand. In this study, we investigate a set of psycholinguistic features that are known to correlate with human processing difficulty (e.g., object relative clauses, long syntactic dependencies, low-frequency n-grams). Using a novel corpus of AI-generated text across diverse domains, we find that AI models use these difficult features more often than paraphrases generated by round-trip translation. Compared with human writing, all nine frontier and near-frontier models use more inanimate subjects with animate verbs and more low-frequency n-grams, and most also use longer dependencies, more stacked nouns, and more reduced object relatives in conversation; we also demonstrate substantial variation across model families. We propose and test a hypothesis as to why: while human language is optimized for successful communication, AI-generated text is increasingly optimized for other goals like math, code, and reasoning, in which there is a pressure for \textit{information density} rather than successful communication. We provide a proof-of-concept for this hypothesis by fine-tuning a language model under a length penalty, which leads to a divergence from human-like linguistic behavior. Our findings highlight the axes of misalignment between linguistic processing demands in humans and LLMs, and point toward possible remedies.

items.title: Researchers develop TraceForge to generate reasoning traces in a student's model style for training large language models, improving coding task performance [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: TraceForge: Distilling with Your Own Thinking
items.summary:
Researchers introduced TraceForge, a two-stage training method that generates reasoning traces in the style of a student's model family using the context and teacher's answer as input. This approach addresses limitations where some models only provide answers without detailed reasoning, which restricts training data generation. TraceForge uses supervised and adversarial training with a generator and critic to produce authentic-looking reasoning traces, achieving higher authenticity scores than real traces on average.

The method was tested on five benchmarks with fixed conditions, showing comparable results on general tasks and outperforming existing reasoning content on coding tasks. Specifically, it improved HumanEval+ by 3.7 points and MBPP+ by 7.1 points at the final checkpoint, with consistent gains throughout training. The researchers suggest that reasoning written in the student's model style facilitates better learning from the generated data.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.29680v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Using an LLM to generate training data for another is among the most general ways to train one, and it remains common practice. Some frontier teams have closed that route for their own models: what comes back is an answer, or a short summary, without the detailed reasoning trace behind it. That is a little ironic: they were themselves built on distilling human knowledge, and distilling an open-source model is still entirely routine; the restriction applies to their own outputs alone. Recent work recovers the hidden reasoning by replaying encrypted blocks across models. It somehow works, but it breaks the providers' terms of service, so it is not something a product can be built on long-term. We built the alternative. We take the context and the teacher's answer as input, and generate the reasoning trace ourselves, in the style of the student's own model family. Training is two-stage, supervised and then adversarial: a generator learns to regenerate the family's own reasoning traces from their context and answer, and a critic learns how real a reasoning trace looks. Applied to a teacher's answer, the generator writes one in the family's style. An independent judge rates how likely traces are to be genuine on a scale from 0 to 1: ours average 0.68, real traces 0.66, and traces selected by the critic from four candidates 0.82. These are authenticity scores, not correctness rates. We test the idea on five benchmarks with everything else held fixed. On general tasks the five training corpora are about the same; on coding, the generated reasoning beats Fable 5's own thinking content. With the same 5,000 questions and the same teacher answers, HumanEval+ improves by 3.7 points and MBPP+ by 7.1 at the final checkpoint, and the MBPP+ lead holds at every checkpoint. We suspect that reasoning written in the student's family style is easier for it to learn from.

items.originalTitle: Parallelizable Probabilistic Latent Reasoning for Diverse Reasoning Trajectories
items.summary: Researchers introduce Probabilistic Latent Reasoning Models (PLRM), a parallelizable variational framework designed to represent and explore diverse reasoning trajectories in a compact latent space. PLRM addresses limitations of existing deterministic and stochastic latent models by enabling parallel inference of latent distributions and modeling multiple reasoning strategies through a mixture-based prior. The approach achieves competitive results on single-trajectory benchmarks and outperforms stochastic baselines on multi-trajectory datasets while reducing training time. PLRM uses a JEPA-style objective with teacher forcing to predict latent distributions and incorporates a discrete strategy variable to preserve the structure of multiple distinct reasoning paths. This work offers a more efficient and flexible method for probabilistic latent reasoning in language models compared to prior autoregressive and deterministic approaches.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.29385v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Language models relying on verbalized Chain-of-Thought (CoT) are constrained to token-by-token generation in the language space, where many tokens serve textual coherence rather than core reasoning. This entangles genuine differences in logical trajectories with superficial variations in verbalization. Moving reasoning into a compact, continuous latent space offers a promising alternative for efficiently representing and exploring diverse reasoning trajectories. However, current latent models remain largely deterministic, capturing only a single reasoning trajectory rather than modeling a distribution over multiple valid alternatives. While stochastic approaches parameterize distributions over latent reasoning steps, they frequently suffer from unstable optimization and limited empirical performance. Furthermore, their reliance on autoregressive latent prediction during training precludes effective parallelization, leading to prohibitively long training times. To overcome these bottlenecks, we propose Probabilistic Latent Reasoning Models (PLRM), a parallelizable variational framework for probabilistic latent reasoning. PLRM adopts a JEPA-style objective in which the posterior infers latent distributions in parallel from observed reasoning trajectories, while the prior learns to predict the subsequent latent distribution via teacher forcing. To model heterogeneous reasoning processes, we introduce a discrete strategy variable together with a mixture-based prior, allowing the model to preserve the Gaussian-mixture structure induced by multiple distinct reasoning trajectories rather than collapsing them into a single Gaussian. Across diverse benchmarks, PLRM achieves performance competitive with deterministic latent reasoning models on single-trajectory datasets while enabling efficient training and consistently outperforming competing stochastic baselines on multi-trajectory datasets.

items.summary: CHIP 2026 Shared Task 1 focused on developing methods to recognize patient-specific phenotype concepts and their associations in full-text biomedical articles. items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.29606v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Automatic phenotype information extraction plays an important role in rare disease diagnosis, genotype-phenotype analysis, and precision medicine. However, accurately identifying phenotype concepts and determining their associations with specific patients remain challenging, particularly in full-text biomedical articles involving multiple patients and complex clinical descriptions. This paper presents an overview of CHIP 2026 Shared Task 1, which aims to promote the development of methods for patient-specific phenotype concept recognition from full-text biomedical literature. The task consists of two subtasks: full-text phenotype concept recognition and patient-specific phenotype association. For this evaluation, we used 200 annotated full-text biomedical articles from the PatientPheX dataset, containing 506 patients, 15,193 phenotype mentions, and 5,656 patient-phenotype associations. A total of 455 teams registered for the competition, with 189 and 103 valid submissions received on the Phase A and Phase B leaderboards, respectively. The best-performing system achieved an overall score of 0.7389 on the final test set, outperforming the baseline by 8.37 percentage points. The top-performing teams explored diverse approaches combining biomedical language models, large language models (LLMs), and ensemble strategies. The evaluation results highlight both the potential of these approaches and the remaining challenges in patient attribution and phenotype normalization from full-text biomedical literature. The post-evaluation phase remains open at https://tianchi.aliyun.com/competition/entrance/532512.

items.title: Researchers propose Code Comprehensor, a hybrid framework combining hierarchical documentation and cross-modal retrieval to improve understanding of large code repositories [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Code Comprehensor: Hierarchical Documentation and Cross-Modal Retrieval for Large Repositories
items.summary: Code Comprehensor integrates CodeGraph, CodeScribe, and CodeContrast to generate hierarchical documentation and enable precise text-to-code retrieval across large codebases. Evaluations on OpenCV and a proprietary 5 million lines of code repository show significant improvements in retrieval accuracy and over 90% faithfulness in LLM-based assessments. The approach addresses challenges in onboarding, maintenance, and impact analysis by providing large language models with richer, context-aware code information.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.30016v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Understanding large, complex, and rapidly evolving code bases remains a core challenge for software engineering at scale, hindering onboarding, maintenance, refactoring, and impact analysis. Providing this information to a Large-Language Model (LLM) is another hurdle, as the LLM must understand not only the required code method but also its associated methods in the grand scheme of the repository. We propose Code Comprehensor, a hybrid retrieval-reasoning framework combining (i) CodeGraph, a code dependency callgraph, (ii) CodeScribe, which uses code-aware LLMs to generate hierarchical documentation across repository call graphs, and (iii) CodeContrast, a CLIP-style dual-encoder model trained on CodeScribe output to learn aligned text-code embeddings. CodeContrast enables fast, semantically precise retrieval of relevant code-context neighborhoods, which serve as grounded evidence for an MCP-based LLM orchestrator answering domain-specific queries. Evaluation on OpenCV and a proprietary 5M-LOC repository shows that CodeScribe-derived supervision significantly improves cross-modal retrieval in text-to-code accuracy over baseline approaches. Richer textual supervision (hierarchical documentation, parent/sibling context, and LLM-generated synthetic questions) consistently enhances performance across both repositories. LLM-as-a-judge evaluation using the popular RAGAS of the Code Comprehensor output yields above 90% faithfulness scores.

items.title: Researchers identify interface-induced trajectory censoring causing mismatches between model outputs and action interfaces, affecting tool-use evaluation scores across multiple benchmarks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Interface-Induced Trajectory Censoring
items.summary:
Researchers studied interface-induced trajectory censoring, a mismatch between model emissions and the interfaces that convert them into actions, which can cause tool-use evaluations to report zero calls despite call-shaped outputs. Experiments on BFCL v4 subsets showed that changing only the serving adapter significantly improved official scorer results without altering model weights. Additional tests across Qwen2.5-Coder checkpoints and tau-bench retail tasks confirmed the phenomenon in both code and non-code environments.

A preregistered 7B LoRA experiment demonstrated that updating the parser increased tool executions dramatically, but did not yield measurable success gains in programmatic or native function-calling evaluations. These findings highlight that tool-use measurements depend heavily on the model-interface configuration and suggest the need for layer-wise observability and conformance checks before attributing evaluation or training outcomes solely to the model.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2609.03966v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Tool-use evaluations typically measure calls through a serving stack, which can report zero calls even when model outputs contain call-shaped payloads. We study interface-induced trajectory censoring: a mismatch between model emissions and the interface that converts them into actions. On selected BFCL v4 subsets, changing only the serving adapter while holding model weights and other evaluation settings fixed moves scores under the official scorer from 0.00 to 0.96 on simple_python and from 0.00 to 0.19 on multi_turn_base. A template-parser factorial experiment shows strong complementarity: neither component replacement alone restores parsing from the baseline, whereas their joint replacement recovers 196/200 first-request parses. Across five Qwen2.5-Coder checkpoints, classifier-positive emissions increase with model size while the mismatched interface reports no calls; a separate matched-interface Qwen3 ladder exhibits few silent emissions through 8B. Experiments on 115 tau-bench retail tasks extend the mechanism to a stateful, non-code environment. In a preregistered, single-seed, 150-step 7B LoRA experiment, changing only the parser registered in verl increases tool executions from 10 to 16,844. However, neither a shared programmatic-feedback evaluation nor a post-hoc common native function-calling evaluation detects a held-out success gain from repair; rescue counts do not increase. Interface repair thus restores tool-mediated experience without a detected performance gain in this setting. These findings show that tool-use measurements depend on the model-interface configuration and motivate layer-wise observability and conformance checks before attributing evaluation or training outcomes to the model alone.

items.originalTitle: Latent Bridges for Multi-Table Question Answering
items.summary: Researchers present GRAB, a pipeline that converts relational data into a heterogeneous graph, encodes it via message passing, and transfers information to a large language model (LLM) through query-conditioned latent tokens. The LLM remains frozen to preserve its reasoning abilities, while only the graph encoder and latent bridge are trained, enabling efficient training with 91 million parameters. This approach significantly enhances performance on relational question answering tasks, especially in complex multi-table scenarios, providing a principled method to integrate relational deep learning with LLMs.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.28916v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We introduce GRAB, a constructor-encoder-bridge pipeline for table question answering. Our method lifts relational data into an heterogeneous graph, encodes it via message passing, and transfers the signals to an LLM through a small set of query-conditioned latent tokens. This provides the LLM with a compact, task-relevant structural representation together with the flattened text. Crucially, the LLM remains strictly frozen to preserve its general reasoning capabilities; we train only the lightweight graph encoder and latent bridge (91M parameters), allowing the entire pipeline to be trained efficiently. Our pipeline significantly improves performance on relational Question Answering, with the largest gains in demanding multi-table settings, offering an efficient, principled way to connect relational deep learning with LLMs.

items.title: Researchers identify scaling laws predicting safety probe performance from model size and label count across multiple language model families [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Scaling Laws for Safety Probes
items.summary: Researchers studied safety probes trained on language model activations to monitor harmful outputs and found that probe error follows two scaling laws related to model size and number of labels. They created six new large safety datasets and trained probes on 20 models from five families, showing that probe error decreases predictably as model size and label count increase. These laws hold across tasks, architectures, and model families, enabling prediction of probe performance and guidance on whether to invest in larger models or more labels for a target error rate. This work helps safety researchers optimize probe design efficiently without extensive retraining.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.30678v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Safety probes trained on a model's activations are a standard tool for monitoring language models in real time. Each time a new model is released or a new harm area needs to be monitored, the probe must be retrained, which requires new labels and a choice of probe architecture. Yet neither the model nor the labels tell us in advance how well the resulting probe will perform. Finding out requires training and comparing many probe configurations. In this paper, we ask whether probe performance can instead be predicted in advance from model size and the number of labels. Existing safety datasets are insufficient for this, as they are either limited in scale or already saturated. We therefore construct six new safety datasets of sufficient size and difficulty. On these datasets, we train two probe architectures on 20 base models from five model families, with 32 to $10^{6}$ labels for each model. We measure performance using probe error, defined as 1 - AUROC, where lower values are better. We find that probe error follows two simple scaling laws. First, the lowest probe error a model can reach falls as a power law in its size. Second, probe error decreases towards its floor as the number of examples increases; the slope increases as the target model size increases. Both laws hold across tasks, model families and probe architectures, and only their fitted constants differ. When fitted on the smallest models of a family, the laws predict the error of the next larger model to within 0.02 in 72% of cases. They also identify whether more labels or a larger model is the cheaper way to reach a target error in 73% of cases. Finally, they choose the probe architecture with an extra error of only 0.006 on average when they pick the worse one. These laws allow safety researchers to determine how to create the best probe for any given model and label budget.

items.originalTitle: Consistency Is Not Validity: Self-Rewarded Moral Argumentation Makes Language Models Decisive but Pliable
items.summary: Researchers developed a reinforcement learning approach where language models judge their own moral arguments to improve performance on ethical decision tasks. Using dilemmas extracted from classic novels and verified by logic solvers, the models learned to rate argument quality similarly to human annotators and became more decisive and invariant to option order on benchmarks like MoralChoice, ELEPHANT, and MORABLES. However, issues such as sycophancy and reframing persisted, indicating that consistency in responses does not necessarily equate to valid moral judgment. Ablation studies confirmed that improvements in consistency could occur without genuine enhancements in moral reasoning, highlighting the complexity of evaluating AI moral judgment.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.30349v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: LLMs are increasingly consulted for moral judgment. We aim to improve performance on such tasks by rewarding good arguments, on the premise that arguing well increases the likelihood of judging well. We train a reinforcement learning policy initialized from a state-of-the-art language model in a self-judged tournament with masked thinking: the generated arguments are judged pairwise on argument quality by the policy itself. As an empirical basis, we extract authentic dilemmas from classic novels, using a logic solver to verify that each constitutes a conflict. We show that our judge rates argument quality like human annotators, and the policy then adopts the language register that it rewards. Testing on the external benchmarks MoralChoice, ELEPHANT, and MORABLES, we find that the policy becomes more decisive and invariant to the order in which options are presented, but sycophancy and reframing remain a challenge to validity. Two ablation studies with synthetic dilemmas and unmasked thinking match the reordering gains, but show a weaker register shift and higher sycophancy. We conclude that consistency is not validity: consistency under reordering can be optimized without improving the moral judgment it is meant to signal.

items.title: Researchers probe and steer safety-relevant behaviors in Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct using activation probes across deception, high-stakes awareness, and sycophancy [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Probing and Steering for Safety-Relevant Behaviours in Large Language Models
items.summary:
Researchers developed activation probes as computed directions in a language model's residual stream to detect and steer safety-relevant behaviors in Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct. They evaluated different estimators, token-pooling schemes, and layers to analyze three behaviors: deception, high-stakes awareness, and sycophancy, finding varying effectiveness depending on the behavior and method used. The study revealed that logistic regression detects behaviors best while difference-of-means steers them best for some behaviors, but this pattern reverses for sycophancy, influenced partly by data rather than estimators.

The team also found that the optimal pooling technique and layer choice depend on the specific behavior and data, with the best steering layer sometimes preceding the best detection layer. They highlighted that metrics for steering a model's perception versus eliciting behavior can differ and may even conflict. The probes and directions developed enable an interactive interface allowing users to score and steer text outputs directly, offering a practical tool for managing safety-related behaviors in large language models.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.30363v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Activation probes are computed directions in a language model's residual stream, used both to detect safety-relevant behaviours and, by adding their direction back into the stream, to steer them. We explore how the main design choices behind such probes interact, within one pipeline, on one model (Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct), and across three behaviours: deception, high-stakes awareness and sycophancy. The pipeline crosses two estimators (difference-of-means and logistic regression) with three token-pooling schemes (last, mean and learned attention), selects appropriate layers to detect or steer a behaviour, and evaluates every direction twice: as a detector of the behaviour, and as a steering vector to push outputs towards the behaviour. Prior work read together suggests a read/write dissociation, in which logistic regression reads (detects) best but difference-of-means directions write (steer) best. We find that it holds for deception and high-stakes but not for sycophancy, where the pattern reverses. The reversal appears to follow partially from the data rather than from the estimators. The best pooling technique and the layer choice depend on the behaviour and data, and the layer that steers best can sit well before the layer that detects best. The right steering metric to use between changing a model's perception and eliciting behaviour depends on the task - and the two can disagree outright. The exported probes and directions power an interactive interface through which a user can score and steer text directly.

items.title: Researchers introduce an atomic interpretable unit framework for evaluating sparse autoencoders, revealing hidden polysemanticity and redundancy in dominant features across multiple architectures
items.originalTitle: Rethinking SAE Evaluation: An Atomic Interpretable Unit Framework Reveals Hidden Polysemanticity and Redundancy
items.summary:
Researchers propose a new evaluation paradigm for sparse autoencoders (SAEs) that requires features to form an atomic interpretable unit basis, aiming to provide a semantically meaningful explanation framework. They organize existing and new metrics, including Dominance-Aware Monosemanticity Evaluation (DAME), into a comprehensive benchmarking system to assess SAE feature sets more effectively.

By evaluating hundreds of SAEs across various architectures and model families, the study uncovers failure modes where SAEs appear monosemantic under current metrics but are functionally polysemantic, with dominant features being less interpretable and more redundant. These findings highlight the need for improved training methods and architectures, and suggest that dominance-aware evaluation should become a standard practice before deploying SAE features for tasks like attribution, circuit tracing, or intervention.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.30474v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) were originally motivated by discovering monosemantic features, a property that characterizes individual features but does not specify what the learned feature set should look like as a whole. As SAEs have increasingly been adopted for attribution, circuit discovery, and intervention, researchers have begun evaluating metrics that describe global properties of the feature set, such as sparsity, dead feature rates, reconstruction fidelity, and disentanglement, a diverse set that extends far beyond monosemanticity. However, this implicit shift beyond monosemanticity has not been formalized as a clear, well-defined objective that comes before these evaluation metrics. Without such an objective, existing metrics remain ad hoc, with their necessity unjustified. In this work, we formalize this ultimate objective by introducing a new paradigm for SAE evaluation: requiring that SAE features, and more generally dictionary-based decompositions of model representations, form an atomic interpretable unit basis, a coordinate system for semantically meaningful explanation. Under this paradigm, we organize existing and new measurements such as DAME (Dominance-Aware Monosemanticity Evaluation) as proxy metrics and introduce a comprehensive benchmarking framework. Evaluating hundreds of SAEs across multiple architectures and model families, we uncover failure modes in which some SAEs appear monosemantic under existing evaluation metrics while remaining functionally polysemantic: the most dominant features, those contributing most to model computation, are systematically less interpretable and more redundant. These failure modes warrant attention from SAE researchers as targets for improved training and architectures, and motivate dominance-aware evaluation as a standard check for practitioners before SAE features are deployed for attribution, circuit tracing, or intervention.

items.title: Researchers find open-book scores in document-level LoRA adapters mainly reflect shared reading behavior rather than unique knowledge retention [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Mostly Reading: What Open-Book Scores Measure in Document-Level LoRA Adapters
items.summary: Researchers trained LoRA adapters on 150 Wikipedia articles using Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct to investigate what open-book scores measure in document-level adapters. They found that open-book scores largely capture a reading behavior common to all adapters, as random adapters trained on different documents recovered 82% of the specialist adapter's open-book advantage but only 2% of its advantage on cloze probes that test factual recall without the source text. Although specialist adapters showed some improvement in cloze recall and their weight updates aligned with the documents they read, tests showed that adapters selected by weight-space proximity or text embedding performed similarly to random adapters on both open-book and cloze probes.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.31017v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Single-document LoRA adapters have been proposed as units of knowledge to be merged and retrieved; yet open-book scoring, with the document in the prompt, can credit a document's own adapter (its specialist) for reading that document as readily as for holding it. Training one adapter for each of 150 Wikipedia articles on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, we find that open-book scores mostly measure a reading behaviour every adapter shares: a random adapter trained on another document recovers 82 % of the specialist's open-book advantage over the base model but only 2 % of its advantage on a cloze probe that asks for the same document's facts without providing the source text, a share we cannot distinguish from zero. Content does reach the weights, since the specialists beat the base model in cloze recall by 0.094, and the geometry of their updates follows the documents they read; yet, in a test of 30 queries, adapters chosen by weight-space proximity or text embedding are not distinguishable from random ones on either probe, although that test cannot exclude an advantage of about four fifths of what a query's own adapter gains over a random one. At 16 documents or more, correctly scaled merges recover 87 % to 89 % of the specialists' open-book advantage but only 12 % to 16 % of their cloze advantage, with intervals that run from below zero to at most 32 %, against 94 % for joint training.We also report four silent errors, each of which produced a clean, wrong result.

items.title: Researchers compare position bias in evidence use across Transformer, state-space, and hybrid Mamba models in long-context question answering tasks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Mixing Matters: Evidence Position Bias Across Sequence Mixers in Long-Context Question Answering
items.summary:
Researchers analyzed how long-context models use answer-bearing evidence depending on its position within a prompt, comparing Transformer, state-space, and hybrid Mamba architectures by moving a gold document among distractors. They found that Transformers show a beginning advantage in using evidence, which state-space models lack, while both favor evidence near the end. Variations in prompt design and dataset affected accuracy and position bias, but the sequence mixer alone was not identified as the sole cause of these effects.

The study observed that attention concentration near initial tokens correlates with beginning sensitivity in Transformers, and that position information remains decodable across architectures despite differing response patterns. These findings suggest that effective context use depends on multiple factors including model family, task, capability, and prompt design, highlighting the complexity of evidence utilization in long-context question answering.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.31135v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Long-context models often use answer-bearing evidence less effectively when it appears away from a prompt boundary. We compare this position bias across Transformer, state-space, and hybrid Mamba architectures by moving one gold document through a fixed set of nine distractors. The evaluated Transformers show a beginning advantage that the evaluated state-space models lack, while both families favor evidence near the end. A matched pure-versus-hybrid Mamba comparison points in the same direction but remains statistically uncertain. The family difference appears among models that can answer the task. Transformer primacy reappears on synthetic retrieval, where state-space ceiling prevents a family comparison. A corpus swap within one state-space architecture changes overall accuracy without a detectable change in curve shape. Prompt changes can create or nearly remove a beginning advantage. Position remains decodable across architectures even when response curves differ, and attention concentration near initial tokens covaries with beginning sensitivity in the tested Transformer family. These exploratory results show that effective context use depends on the evaluated architecture family, capability, task, and prompt, without isolating the sequence mixer as the sole cause.

items.title: Researchers find tool-augmented language models increase accuracy but also widen prompt sensitivity in model comparisons across multiple domains and wordings [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Prompt Sensitivity in Tool-Augmented Model Comparisons
items.summary:
Researchers studied how equipping language models with external tools affects the stability of model comparisons on question-answering benchmarks with varied question wordings. They developed a protocol separating reasoning, tool use, and answer reporting steps, applying it to six open models across five domains and five question formulations. The study found that while tools improve accuracy when programs answer questions, they also increase sensitivity to prompt wording in many pairwise model comparisons, influenced by how often models call tools and the interface design.

The sensitivity varied depending on the tool-calling interface and instructions; for example, a native tool interface and a second tool description eliminated detected sensitivity in molecular tasks, whereas sensitivity persisted when tools returned intermediate results. These results indicate that deterministic answer reports do not guarantee stable model comparisons, leading the researchers to recommend reporting both tool call frequency and comparison stability across multiple prompt wordings alongside accuracy metrics.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.31148v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Language models are compared on question-answering benchmarks that pose each question in one wording, and a reworded question can change which of two models scores higher. We ask whether giving the models tools makes such comparisons more stable. An accuracy gain cannot answer this, because tools change several steps between the question and the scored answer at once. We propose a matched protocol that separates those steps: the answer readout, reasoning, the decision to call, the tool's answer, and the report supplied without a call. We apply it to six open models in five domains under five wordings. We find that tools raise accuracy where a program answers the question and widen the wording sensitivity of many pairwise comparisons. The widening follows how often a model calls, and call frequency follows the wording for some models and not others. It also depends on the interface and the instructions: a native tool-calling interface and a second tool description leave no detected widening in molecules, and sensitivity persists where tools return intermediate results. These findings show that deterministic reports do not guarantee stable comparisons. We recommend reporting call frequency and comparison stability under several wordings beside accuracy.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.31172v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: LLM-as-a-Judge evaluation is increasingly applied to multilingual tasks, yet prompting strategies such as Chain-of-Thought and Role Conditioning are recommended based solely on English benchmarks. Whether their effectiveness transfers across judge models and languages remains unknown: prompt-sensitivity studies are largely English-centric, while existing multilingual judge studies fix the prompt template. In this work, we address this gap by measuring this interaction through a benchmark of 9 prompting strategies, 4 open-weight judges, 27 languages, and 4 tasks across 13 datasets, yielding over 1M pointwise scores on gold-reference outputs, validated against human judgments. We find that prompting strategies are not transferable: the choice of the judge model dominates the choice of prompting strategy, strategy effects reverse direction across judges, and stability degrades in low-resource languages, where these effects are concealed by aggregate reporting. These findings show that prompting effects in multilingual evaluation are conditioned on the judge, task, and language. Consequently, prompting strategies should be validated for the intended evaluation setting, and cross-study comparisons should account for both judge and prompt configuration.

items.title: When More Metadata Misleads: Probing Field-Level Grounding in LLM-Generated Museum Descriptions [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: When More Metadata Misleads: Probing Field-Level Grounding in LLM-Generated Museum Descriptions
items.summary: arXiv:2610.31193v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Metadata-conditioned generation is often framed as a data-to-text task in which additional input fields should improve grounding. Museum description generation challenges this assumption because catalogue records are heterogeneous, partially visual, and unevenly documented across geographic regions. We study how metadata composition shapes the generation of artefact descriptions through a two-phase framework. Phase 1 analyses natural metadata variation in a large museum collection, where field count, field type, image availability, and Place co-vary. Phase 2 introduces controlled field probes that hold object identity fixed while varying metadata quantity, field type, and image access. Our results show that metadata quantity alone does not explain generation behaviour. Field type determines whether models ground, omit, or infer information, while images can both support visual grounding and increase unsupported interpretation. More broadly, our findings show that metadata-conditioned data-to-text evaluation should assess field- and claim-level support, rather than relying only on aggregate input coverage or reference similarity.

items.title: HERD: Harness-Evolving Recursive Distillation for Continual Learning [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: HERD: Harness-Evolving Recursive Distillation for Continual Learning
items.summary: arXiv:2610.31401v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Continual learning requires a model to keep acquiring new skills and knowledge without compromising its existing capabilities. Parametric methods suffer from catastrophic forgetting and loss of plasticity. Non-parametric methods, such as prompts, skills, and harnesses, leverage in-context learning but are limited by context length and lossy plain-text compression. To effectively combine their complementary strengths, we propose HERD (Harness-Evolving Recursive Distillation), a hybrid continual learning framework that learns efficiently in the harness and internalizes experience into cumulative capabilities via distillation. On the harness side, HERD continually refines its skills to capture reusable patterns, while retaining high-residual examples that the skills fail to capture in a bounded memory. On the parameter side, HERD performs drift-constrained distillation with dual anchors, substantially reducing forgetting over long recursive runs. On the 25-stage task stream of TRACE+17, under fixed memory and compute budgets, HERD matches the strongest parametric baseline in new-task acquisition while exhibiting the least forgetting and the strongest retention of general capabilities.

items.title: How Depth Growth and Looping Shape In-Context Learning in Language Models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: How Depth Growth and Looping Shape In-Context Learning in Language Models
items.summary: arXiv:2610.31421v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Looped and depth-grown language models reuse computations across depth and have attracted interest for their reasoning capabilities. Building on prior suggestive evidence of improved in-context-learning (ICL), we investigate how such reuse favors ICL, including how it shapes the acquisition, retention, and mechanisms of this ability. Our analysis spans pretrained language models up to 3B parameters and controlled tasks. The experiments provide evidence for a shared inductive bias toward learning from context: grown and looped models rely more on information in context and, compared with a full-depth dense reference, acquire ICL earlier in controlled tasks and retain it more strongly when learning fixed associations in the weights is also possible. Tracing attention heads through training reveals that depth growth propagates early induction heads across layers. Ablations show that grown and looped models rely more strongly on induction-ranked heads for both few-shot performance and later-token prediction. Together, these findings provide evidence for a shared inductive bias toward learning from context and suggest that (soft) parameter reuse shapes how this ability develops and which attention mechanisms support it.

items.title: Would an LLM Match into a Residency? Uncertainty, Reasoning and Image Use of Open Language Models on the Spanish MIR Examination [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Would an LLM Match into a Residency? Uncertainty, Reasoning and Image Use of Open Language Models on the Spanish MIR Examination
items.summary: arXiv:2610.31586v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Accuracy on medical examinations is common evidence offered for the clinical use of language models, yet a health system that intends to run an open model on its own hardware needs to know considerably more: whether the model recognizes when it is likely to be wrong, whether medical fine-tuning improves this ability, whether its correct answers rest on sound clinical reasoning, or whether it actually uses the images it is given. We examine these questions for four open models of 8 to 27 billion parameters on the Spanish MIR residency examination, scoring 1,552 questions from eight editions under the exam's own rules. Answering every question, the three larger models would rank among roughly the first 600 to 3,000 candidates, with 41 to 43 specialties still open to them. Abstention, however, never pays, because even their least confident answers are right more often than the 25% break-even. Medical fine-tuning reduced overconfidence at the cost of accuracy, without improving how well confidence separates right from wrong answers. Moreover, 13-38% of correct answers rejected a distractor for a clinically unsound reason that confidence did not reflect, and removing or swapping the provided contextual images left accuracy unchanged.

items.title: Cost-Aware Abstention for LLM-Based IT Ticket Classification
items.originalTitle: Cost-Aware Abstention for LLM-Based IT Ticket Classification
items.summary: arXiv:2610.31657v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Wrong automatic routing of an IT support ticket can cost more than human triage. We evaluate cost-aware abstention as an offline, cost-conditional readiness assessment: select a routing policy on calibration data under explicit costs, then evaluate that frozen policy once on held-out test data. On a public 47,837-ticket, eight-class corpus, we compare four trained non-LLM classifiers with four large language models under zero- and few-shot prompting. Under the illustrative cost model (c_ok, c_triage, c_wrong) = (0, 1, 5), TF-IDF with logistic regression and a threshold of 0.60 selected on calibration reduces test cost from 0.763 to 0.472, a 38.1% relative reduction (paired ratio-bootstrap 95% CI [35.7%, 40.4%]), while lowering wrong routes from 15.3% to 3.5%. Frozen calibration-selected policies also beat both always-route and always-defer on held-out test data in 14 of 16 settings in a post-hoc cost-parameter analysis. The strongest prompted configuration reaches 0.477 accuracy on a stratified 1,000-ticket test subset, versus 0.879 for fine-tuned DistilBERT on the same tickets. Isotonic lowers expected calibration error without reliably improving discrimination: GPT-4o-mini few-shot has one confidence value before and after recalibration and correctness AUROC 0.500. We therefore report correctness AUROC and tie-aware risk-coverage area alongside ECE. At the analytically derived break-even probability 0.80, seven prompted configurations defer all tickets; Haiku few-shot routes only 19/1,000. An LLM-only agreement control and margin/entropy rejection baselines further separate calibration from discrimination. The findings are scoped to this dataset, prompt design, model endpoints, and illustrative costs; the work is an evaluation framework, not a new abstention algorithm or universal deployment certification.

items.summary: arXiv:2602.03358v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Finding effective prompts for language models (LMs) is critical yet notoriously difficult: the prompt space is combinatorially large, rewards are sparse due to expensive target-LM evaluation. Yet, existing RL-based prompt optimizers often rely on on-policy updates and a meta-prompt sampled from a fixed distribution, leading to poor sample efficiency. We propose GFlowPO, a probabilistic prompt optimization framework that casts prompt search as a posterior inference problem over latent prompts regularized by a meta-prompted reference-LM prior. In the first step, we fine-tune a lightweight prompt-LM with an off-policy Generative Flow Network (GFlowNet) objective, using a replay-based training policy that reuses past prompt evaluations to enable sample-efficient exploration. In the second step, we introduce Dynamic Memory Update (DMU), a training-free mechanism that updates the meta-prompt by injecting both (i) diverse prompts from a replay buffer and (ii) top-performing prompts from a small priority queue, thereby progressively concentrating the search process on high-reward regions. Across few-shot text classification, instruction induction benchmarks, and question answering tasks, GFlowPO consistently outperforms recent discrete prompt optimization baselines.

items.title: When Self-Consistency Backfires: Majority Vote Hurts the Majority of Hard Science Problems for Small LLMs
items.originalTitle: When Self-Consistency Backfires: Majority Vote Hurts the Majority of Hard Science Problems for Small LLMs
items.summary: arXiv:2608.11403v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Majority-vote self-consistency (SC) lowers per-problem accuracy on most GPQA Diamond problems for small instruction-tuned models: on 56.6% of problems for Qwen2.5-7B and 65.7% for Llama-3-8B. An obvious fix is a verifier-free confidence gate that decides which problems to vote on. We report that the most natural version of that fix also fails, and we separate three signal failures that v1 treated as one. The token-entropy gate fails for a measurement reason: averaged over a chain of 602 tokens, entropy mostly measures fluency. The chain average sits 0.0005 nats from the non-answer average and 0.1695 nats from the answer token. So we measure confidence at the answer token itself. On Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct-Turbo (198 problems, 64 samples each), a sample that disagrees with its problem's plurality still emits its answer at a median margin of at least 20.4 nats, and at least 75.5% of such samples exceed 10 nats. Both quantities were pre-registered and tested once on 69 problems that no exploratory analysis had seen; both passed. The unit matters. Pooled across the benchmark, the margin does separate correct from incorrect samples: the fraction above 10 nats differs by +0.0586 [+0.0160, +0.0994]. Within a problem, paired, it does not: -0.0142 [-0.0501, +0.0215]. Token log-probabilities do carry information, but not for the within-question choice that self-consistency makes. The agreement gate's failure has no mechanism we can identify, and we leave it open. The new claims rest on one model: a registered replication on a second model was sampled but could not be evaluated, and we report that instead. Separately, three reasoning models could not be evaluated on hosted serverless inference at a small budget, each for a different measured reason. All three are downloadable, so this is a limit of metered APIs, not of what can be known.

items.title: ShIOEnv: A Command Evaluation Environment for Grammar-Constrained Synthesis and Execution Behavior Modeling [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: ShIOEnv: A Command Evaluation Environment for Grammar-Constrained Synthesis and Execution Behavior Modeling
items.summary: arXiv:2505.18374v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We introduce ShIOEnv, a Gymnasium-compatible Bash environment for synthesizing execution-annotated shell input traces. Datasets containing such traces are useful for training models to perform execution-free shell simulation, which in turn is useful for deploying honeypots for cyber deception. Existing datasets, such as NL2CMD and other Bash command corpora, do not include complete execution artifacts (stdout, stderr, exit status, and changes to the system's state) associated with a command's execution. ShIOEnv synthesizes shell inputs, executes them in a controlled system context, and records stdout, stderr, exit status, and structured filesystem and environment patches. Unconstrained (random) generation of shell inputs (command and arguments) results in multiple instances of arguments that are mostly redundant or result in execution errors. We introduce grammar-constrained synthesis to generate syntactically valid arguments with high input irreducibility, which we estimate through self-ablative contrasts of execution artifacts. We prepare 1.6M samples using grammar-constrained and unconstrained synthesis and collect their execution artifacts for 86 Linux/Bash utilities. Using this dataset, we train small language models (CodeT5) and evaluate their accuracy in predicting the actual execution behavior of attacker-sourced Bash commands. These models outperform commonly used rule-based simulation (Cowrie) and prompted large language models by up to 14.2 pp in output edit similarity (O-ES). We enhance the NL2CMD dataset by constructing 500K samples executable in a grounded system context along with their complete execution artifacts. We empirically demonstrate that models trained on grammar-constrained samples outperform those trained on NL2CMD samples by 22.5 pp in O-ES. ShIOEnv, command grammars, and 2.1M samples used in our primary evaluations are released for use by other researchers.

items.title: FLAWS: A Benchmark for Error Identification and Localization in Scientific Papers [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: FLAWS: A Benchmark for Error Identification and Localization in Scientific Papers
items.summary: arXiv:2511.21843v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The identification and localization of errors is a core task in peer review, yet the exponential growth of scientific output has made it increasingly difficult for human reviewers to reliably detect errors given the limited pool of experts. Recent advances in Large Language Models (LLMs) have sparked interest in their potential to support such evaluation tasks, from academic peer review to automated scientific assessment. However, despite the growing use of LLMs in review systems, their capabilities to pinpoint errors remain underexplored. In this work, we introduce Fault Localization Across Writing in Science (FLAWS), an automated benchmark consisting of 713 paper-error pairs designed to evaluate how effectively LLMs detect errors that undermine key claims in research papers. We construct the benchmark by systematically inserting claim-invalidating errors into peer-reviewed papers using LLMs, paired with an automated evaluation metric that measures whether models can identify and localize these errors. Developing such a benchmark presents unique challenges that we overcome: ensuring that the inserted errors are well-defined, challenging, and relevant to the content of the paper, avoiding artifacts that would make identification trivial, and designing a scalable, automated evaluation metric. On the resulting benchmark, we evaluate five frontier LLMs: Claude Sonnet 4.5, DeepSeek Reasoner v3.1, Gemini 2.5 Pro, GPT 5, and Grok 4. Among these, GPT 5 is the top-performing model, achieving 39.1% identification accuracy when k=10, where k is the number of top-ranked error text candidates generated by the LLM.

items.title: Markovian Generation Chains in Large Language Models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Markovian Generation Chains in Large Language Models
items.summary: arXiv:2603.11228v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The widespread use of large language models (LLMs) raises an important question: how do texts evolve when they are repeatedly processed by LLMs? In this paper, we define this iterative inference process as Markovian generation chains, where each step takes a specific prompt template and the previous output as input, without including any prior data. In iterative rephrasing and round-trip translation experiments, the output either converges to a small recurrent set or continues to produce novel sentences within a finite horizon. Through sentence-level Markov chain modeling and analysis of simulated data, we show that iterative process can either increase or reduce the diversity depending on factors such as the temperature parameter and the initial input sentence. These results offer valuable insights into the dynamics of iterative LLM inference and their implications for multi-agent LLM systems.

items.title: AtManRL: Towards Faithful Reasoning via Differentiable Attention Saliency [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: AtManRL: Towards Faithful Reasoning via Differentiable Attention Saliency
items.summary: arXiv:2604.16158v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly rely on chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning to solve complex tasks, yet a reasoning trace may merely accompany the final answer rather than causally contribute to it or faithfully reflect how it was reached. We introduce differentiable attention manipulation to train salient reasoning with reinforcement learning -- method which we call AtManRL. By optimizing an additive attention mask that identifies the CoT tokens needed to recover the model's answer, we derive a saliency reward and combine it with an outcome reward in GRPO with decoupled advantages. Because both saliency and faithfulness depend strongly on trace length, we evaluate against a sweep of length-penalty baselines that traces the trade-off a pure length penalty can reach, rather than against a single baseline. Across three models (Qwen2.5-3B, Granite-3.3-2B, and Phi-4-mini) and four benchmarks (GSM8K, MMLU, ProofWriter, and QuestBench), AtManRL sits above this trade-off curve by 3.9-4.0pp in saliency, measured as answer changes under mistake injection, and by 5.7-7.7pp in faithfulness, measured as hint verbalization under hint injection, while matching the accuracy of baselines of similar length. These results suggest that training explicitly for saliency is a promising route towards chain-of-thought reasoning that is more faithful to the model's actual decision process.

We introduce differentiable attention manipulation to train salient reasoning with reinforcement learning -- method which we call AtManRL. By optimizing an additive attention mask that identifies the CoT tokens needed to recover the model's answer, we derive a saliency reward and combine it with an outcome reward in GRPO with decoupled advantages. Because both saliency and faithfulness depend strongly on trace length, we evaluate against a sweep of length-penalty baselines that traces the trade-off a pure length penalty can reach, rather than against a single baseline. Across three models (Qwen2.5-3B, Granite-3.3-2B, and Phi-4-mini) and four benchmarks (GSM8K, MMLU, ProofWriter, and QuestBench), AtManRL sits above this trade-off curve by 3.9-4.0pp in saliency, measured as answer changes under mistake injection, and by 5.7-7.7pp in faithfulness, measured as hint verbalization under hint injection, while matching the accuracy of baselines of similar length. These results suggest that training explicitly for saliency is a promising route towards chain-of-thought reasoning that is more faithful to the model's actual decision process.

items.title: Graph Memory Transformer (GMT) [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Graph Memory Transformer (GMT)
items.summary: arXiv:2604.23862v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We investigate whether an explicit learned memory graph can replace the Feed-Forward Network (FFN) sublayer in a decoder-only transformer while preserving the surrounding autoregressive architecture. In the proposed graph Memory Transformer (GMT), a memory cell routes token representations over a learned bank of centroids connected by a learned directed transition matrix, while causal self-attention remains unchanged. In the base v7 instantiation, each of 16 transformer blocks contains 128 centroids and a 128 x 128 edge matrix. Each cell uses gravitational source routing and token-conditioned target selection to return a gated displacement from the estimated source memory state toward the target memory state, rather than a retrieved value. The resulting decoder-only language model has 82.2M trainable parameters and no dense FFN sublayers; the evaluated dense GPT-style baseline has 103.0M. It trains stably and exposes centroid usage, transition structure, and source-to-target movement for direct inspection in the forward computation. It trails the larger baseline in validation loss and perplexity (3.5995/36.58 vs. 3.2903/26.85), while showing close zero-shot benchmark behavior under the evaluated setting. These results support the viability and structural interpretability of replacing dense within-token transformation with graph-mediated memory navigation, without claiming state-of-the-art performance. Broader scaling, optimized kernels, and more extensive benchmark evaluation remain for future work.

items.title: When Should LLMs Reason? Adaptive Inference Routing via Entropy Dynamics [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: When Should LLMs Reason? Adaptive Inference Routing via Entropy Dynamics
items.summary: arXiv:2605.22873v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning can improve LLM performance, but its benefits vary across tasks, models, and individual queries. On some tasks, CoT provides marginal or negative accuracy gains while substantially increasing token consumption. We investigate whether early decoding dynamics can help identify when explicit reasoning is useful. Our analysis shows that tasks with larger CoT gains tend to exhibit decreasing early-stage entropy, while low-gain tasks more often show oscillatory or increasing trajectories. These patterns motivate an empirical regime interpretation of decoding behavior. We propose \textbf{EDRM} (Entropy Dynamics-based Reasoning Manifold), a lightweight routing framework whose default heuristic requires no router training. EDRM summarizes early entropy trajectories with a compact, interpretable representation and selects among Direct, Standard, and CoT decoding. Across 15 benchmarks and 7 LLMs, its global and instance-level variants offer \textbf{16--55\%} token savings at comparable accuracy. The Full instance-level configuration combines routing with a short Direct fallback branch; our heuristic-router ablation reports up to \textbf{4.9 percentage points} of additional accuracy from oracle answer selection over routing without fallback. These results support selective reasoning based on early decoding signals and demonstrate the potential of entropy-based control for efficient LLM inference.

items.title: Rubric Dropout: A Simple Way to Mitigate Reward Hacking in Rubric-Based RL [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Rubric Dropout: A Simple Way to Mitigate Reward Hacking in Rubric-Based RL
items.summary: arXiv:2608.11669v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Rubric-based reinforcement learning, in which an LLM judge scores responses against prompt-specific criteria, has become a standard way to post-train language models on tasks without verifiable answers. The rubric, however, is only a proxy for response quality, and a policy trained against it long enough learns to exploit the difference. We train models with GRPO on medical and science rubrics and grade their responses on out-of-distribution (OOD) benchmarks throughout training with two judges: the training judge and a stronger OOD judge. The two scores first rise together and then diverge. The policy is learning to satisfy the training judge without writing better responses, which is a form of reward hacking. To mitigate it, we propose Rubric Dropout, which applies dropout to rubric criteria: at each training step, a random subset of each rubric's criteria is removed from the reward, so the rewarded subset of criteria is resampled at each step. All responses sampled for the same prompt are scored on the same subset, so their rewards remain comparable, and evaluation always uses the full rubric. We also introduce Block Dropout, which drops semantically similar criteria together so that a near duplicate of a dropped criterion cannot keep rewarding the same behavior. Across both benchmarks and models from 1.7B to 8B, dropout improves the gold judge's score on OOD benchmarks by up to 3 percent on HealthBench-Hard and 7 percent on ResearchQA, and it reduces both the gap between the two judges and over-crediting. It keeps in-domain reward close to the baseline, and dropout rates of 30-50 percent work best. Block Dropout improves the gold judge's OOD score further at the same dropout rate. Changing which criteria are rewarded at each step is a simple, inexpensive way to make rubric rewards harder to exploit.

items.title: Moving the Mean Toward the Known Good, Not Beyond It: What Inference-Time Interventions and Weight Consolidation Buy in Open-Ended Generation [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Moving the Mean Toward the Known Good, Not Beyond It: What Inference-Time Interventions and Weight Consolidation Buy in Open-Ended Generation
items.summary: arXiv:2608.28886v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: What does a generation loop gain from learning on its own verified successes? In cycles of generate, verify, select and LoRA-consolidate on online bin packing, training on value-filtered candidates shifts what the model writes on held-out variants toward value (-1.7 points of excess, p=0.008; -3.1 against a random-consolidation control, p=0.004) while the best observed candidate converges to the classic heuristic's level and no further. A confirmation battery replicates the whole procedure three times, with fresh seeds and a never-consulted held-out set read exactly once: the mean was nearly identical in all three lineages (-2.0, -1.8, -1.9), and after aggregating within held-out variant all seven evaluable variants favored consolidation (p=0.008). The best observed candidate moved to the classic heuristic's level, exactly (0.021028, the lowest variant's classic level, in all three lineages and both arms); attract never went beyond its variant's classic level, while the random control did in 7 of 24 lineage-variant cells. A matched SFT-only control shows the supervised anchor, not repulsion from bad candidates, does the concentrating (96% of candidates land exactly at the classic heuristic's level). On far families the tails cut both ways: consolidation lowers the per-candidate rate of better-than-classic candidates (10% to 3.9%) while its larger production yields more such candidates absolutely (5 against 1, on few events). As motivation we report the inference-time ledger that led here: a model-written schematic recap buys judged document integration and nothing buys development; a verifier written into the stream is imitated, 16.4 fabricated verdict lines per notebook. In this arrangement (an 8-bit model in MLX, five cycles), mean quality among valid candidates can be bought and replicated; under attraction the observed best goes to the classic and, so far, never beyond it.

items.title: Operator Packages, Proposer Strength, and Construction-Family Plateaus in Office-Scale Verified Search [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Operator Packages, Proposer Strength, and Construction-Family Plateaus in Office-Scale Verified Search
items.summary: arXiv:2609.29636v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Verified search, in which a language model proposes programs, a hard evaluator scores them, and selection keeps the best, has recently moved mathematical records; controlled ablations of the proposer-side components remain rare. We instrument a minimal FunSearch-style loop at office scale (a 30B local model on a laptop, 120-600 verified samples per run) with three operator packages: a schematic notebook the model writes and carries instead of verbatim elites, a named obstacle, and behavioural repulsion from constructions already found. On nine construction problems from a public repository, the complete 2^3 factorial with two replicates favours the primary contrast in a nominal two-stage analysis: the composition closes more of the seed-to-record gap (+0.196; nominal pooled p=0.023, stage-combination p~0.08; median per-problem effect +0.045). Repulsion raises construction-hash diversity in eight of nine problems (one-sided p=0.0039; partly a manipulation check). items.title: StochIKM: Automated High-Fidelity Reconstruction of Individual Patient Data from Published Kaplan-Meier Curves [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: StochIKM: Automated High-Fidelity Reconstruction of Individual Patient Data from Published Kaplan-Meier Curves
items.summary: arXiv:2610.29122v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Individual patient data are the gold standard for secondary analysis of time-to-event evidence, but they are rarely released, and reconstruction from a published Kaplan-Meier figure could help. Existing methods all claim high fidelity, each judged by whichever agreements it happens to achieve, and each returns a single dataset although the map from figure to data is not bijective. We define fidelity explicitly: a dataset is admissible when it reproduces the risk table exactly, follows the digitized curve to within the image resolution, and respects the printed median, interval and event count. We propose StochIKM, a stochastic algorithm that digitizes the figure with a vision-capable language model and uses the high-fidelity definition as constraints, returning an admissible set of individual patient datasets. A solution is guaranteed to exist whenever the figure has been read correctly, so a failure indicts either the published figure or its digitization. In simulation and in 79 arms from published oncology trials, StochIKM reproduces the published risk tables and medians more closely than LLM-improved IPDfromKM, a high-impact alternative.

items.title: When Multiple Choices Are Correct: Asymmetric Probability Allocation in Jev and Other Decision Models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: When Multiple Choices Are Correct: Asymmetric Probability Allocation in Jev and Other Decision Models
items.summary: arXiv:2610.29217v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Decision models return normalized probability distributions over candidate choices, which downstream applications can use to select among choices. Although their providers emphasize the reliability of these probabilities, calibration on tasks with a single correct choice does not establish their reliability when multiple choices are correct. We evaluate three decision models (Jev, Liquid d1, and GPT-6 Luna Decisions) on three diverse datasets (MetaTool, HotpotQA, and ECtHR) to study probability allocation and thresholding. Even when models rank every correct choice above every distractor, in 28% to 50% of those lists, at least one correct choice receives a probability below the uniform probability of 1/n, where n is the number of choices. We also present each model with five identical copies of a correct choice and observe probability disparities, with mean gaps ranging from 17 to 79 percentage points. We further show how these allocation disparities affect the recovery of multiple correct choices under probability thresholding. Decision-model probabilities can rank correct choices, but a probability threshold does not identify the set of correct choices.

items.title: AgentMonopoly: Behavioral Patterns and Persona Control in LLM Agents [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: AgentMonopoly: Behavioral Patterns and Persona Control in LLM Agents
items.summary: arXiv:2610.29330v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: How do LLM agents' strategies differ, and how much can instructions to adopt a persona change their behavior over a game? We study these questions with AgentMonopoly, an environment where agents communicate, buy and trade properties, and make decisions that affect later turns. We compare models from four families, each at two sizes, in games with identical models, different sizes of the same family, or different families. We also assign one agent a persona, a description of how it should behave, intended to change a tendency observed in games without that persona. The tested models differ in how often they trade, waive rent, and manage cash and properties. Larger models do not consistently win more games. Persona instructions change the words agents use and some of their actions, but the changes do not always match the role across all decisions. These results show why persona following should be assessed through actions and outcomes as well as language. As our findings are conditional on the tested checkpoints, prompts, and five seeds per configuration, the open-source nature of AgentMonopoly provides the experimental infrastructure for further extending these comparisons. Our code is available at https://github.com/SuELS-Group/Agent_Monopoly.

items.title: OpenMAP-HIE: Pathology Informed Score-based Diffusion Model for Unsupervised Neonatal Hypoxic-Ischemic Encephalopathy Lesion Segmentation [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: OpenMAP-HIE: Pathology Informed Score-based Diffusion Model for Unsupervised Neonatal Hypoxic-Ischemic Encephalopathy Lesion Segmentation
items.summary: arXiv:2610.29322v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Accurate localization of neonatal hypoxic--ischemic encephalopathy (HIE) lesions on apparent diffusion coefficient (ADC) images is clinically important but is limited by scarce expert annotations and substantial variation in lesion appearance. We propose OpenMAP-HIE, a pathology-informed score-based diffusion model for unsupervised HIE lesion localization without voxel-wise lesion supervision. A denoising diffusion model learns the healthy neonatal ADC distribution, while a ControlNet-based conditional branch preserves patient-specific anatomy. At inference, anomaly evidence is derived directly from differences between conditional and unconditioned noise predictions at independently evaluated diffusion noise levels, avoiding dependence on a final pseudo-healthy reconstruction or sequential reverse-diffusion chain. Based on the characteristic ADC reduction associated with acute HIE, only discrepancies consistent with the expected pathological direction are retained and aggregated across noise levels using a geometric mean. Spatial mean filtering further suppresses isolated responses. The framework was evaluated on the BONBID-HIE dataset. The ADC-only method achieved a Dice score of $0.283\pm0.244$, average precision of $0.505$, Hausdorff distance of $25.45\pm15.63$ mm, mean average surface distance of $9.40\pm8.49$ mm, and normalized surface distance of $0.355\pm0.236$, providing the best overlap and surface-distance performance among the evaluated unsupervised methods and Dice performance comparable to supervised ADC-only models. Optional population-derived ADC $Z$-map refinement further increased Dice to $0.602\pm0.269$. These findings support pathology-informed score discrepancies as a useful signal for neonatal HIE lesion localization, while highlighting remaining challenges in detecting small and low-contrast lesions.
